title: What it is not
hookLine: the Abhidhamma is one way of looking, not a test anyone must pass

lines: AN OLD MAN WITHOUT THE BOOKS.
cards: Fifty-two mental factors. Twenty-eight kinds of matter. Twenty-four conditions.
After all these lists, a fair question rises up: does a person have to learn all this? Is there an exam at the end of the path, a long sheet of Pali with blanks to fill in?
The Theravada tradition has its own answer, and it comes in a story about an old man who never opened the books.

teach.b: First, two duties. In the commentary on the Dhammapada, a man who has become a monk late in life asks the Buddha what the duties are in this teaching. There are two, the story says.
One is the duty of the books: learning the texts, studying, keeping the words. The other is the duty of insight: watching body and mind until you see how they really are.

teach.h: THE OLD MONK CHOOSES THE SITTING.
teach.b: Second, the old monk chooses. In paraphrase: I came to this late, I'm too old for the books, teach me the second.
He's taught a meditation practice and goes off to sit, and the story goes on to tell how far he went with it. Nobody in the story tells him he chose wrong.

Both duties are honored, and the Theravada tradition has kept both: monks and lay people who study the lists closely, and monks and lay people whose whole practice is the sitting. Third, the lists aren't one fixed answer.
The Sarvastivada, the other school, counts some things differently.
Two careful traditions, looking at the same mind, drew two maps. A map is a way of looking. It isn't the ground you walk on.
Fourth, what that leaves. The Abhidhamma is a gift some people love: precise, patient, endless. For others it's a mirror they pick up now and then.
For some it never comes off the shelf. None of that is a pass or a fail.

teach.h: A WAY OF LOOKING, NOT A TEST.
teach.b: The test, if there is one, is the old monk's: does the looking help you see?

how: In Theravada communities, some monks and lay people devote years to studying the Abhidhamma, while others give their practice mainly to meditation; the tradition honors both study and insight.

games.q: what does “what it is not” mean?
o: the lists were dropped by later Theravada
the lists are only for monks, not lay people
the lists are one way of looking, not an exam

games.q: one way of looking: tap the pairs.
p: drew two maps of the same mind

s: the Abhidhamma is a test every Buddhist must pass
it's one way of looking. the tradition honors both the duty of the books and the duty of insight.
in the story, the old monk is told he chose wrong
nobody tells him that. he's taught a meditation practice and goes off to sit.
two early schools counted some things differently
the Sarvastivada's Abhidharma and the Theravada Abhidhamma drew different maps of the same mind.

games.q: you've come to the path late in life, and the Buddha tells you there are two duties, the books and insight. which do you take?
o: the books: learn every list first
insight: teach me to sit and see
neither: it's too late to start
games.why: the old monk in the Dhammapada commentary says he's too old for the books and asks for the second. nobody tells him he chose wrong.

practice: Rest one hand open on your knee, palm up and loose, as if a small list were lying in it that you could close your fingers around or let slide off.
Sit with the breath, and if a name comes, restless, calm, doubt, let it sit on the open palm without gripping it or throwing it away.

wordCard.voice: What it is not. The Abhidhamma isn't an exam the path sets. It's one way of looking, honored alongside the duty of simply sitting and seeing. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: one way of looking. The books and the sitting are both honored, and neither is a test. Rest well.

sources.ref: Dhammapada commentary on verse 1 (the story of the elder Cakkhupala), the two duties
